teach.title: Where something comes from
teach.say: To say where somebody comes from, or is leaving, Latin uses *ex* (out of), *ab* (away from) or *dē* (down from, about) and changes the noun's ending. That ending is **the ablative (the 'from' form)**: *ex vīllā* — out of the house. It answers *unde?*, from where?

check.ask: Which word says where the boys come from?

teach.title: The endings are the ones you already know
teach.say: Nothing new to learn in the noun: after *ex* a word in -a ends -ā and a word in -us or -um ends -ō, exactly as after *in*. *Ex vīllā*, *ex hortō*, *ex ātriō*. Only the preposition tells you the meaning has turned from 'in' to 'out of'.

show.say: ex ātriō — -um becomes -ō, the same ending as after *in*

teach.title: *ab* — away from a person or a thing
teach.say: *Ab* is 'away from': *ab ōstiō* — from the door, *ab Aemiliā* — away from Aemilia. Before a consonant Ørberg writes it ā, with no b, but it is the same word and the same case.

teach.title: *dē* keeps the case even when it means 'about'
teach.say: *Dē* began as 'down from' and is now mostly 'about, concerning' — but the ending never changes with the meaning: *dē fīliō suō* is 'about her son', and *fīliō* is the same 'from' form as in *ex hortō*. Learn the preposition, and the case comes with it.

check.ask: Is *rosīs* the 'from' form, and what put it there?

teach.title: The preposition decides, not the ending
teach.say: *In hortō* and *ex hortō* are the same word with the same ending, and they mean opposite things. The ablative on its own does not say 'in' or 'out of'; the little word in front does. Read the preposition first, then the ending.

check.ask: Does *vīllā* here say where they are or where they come from?

teach.title: Several places, and *sine*
teach.say: For more than one the ending is -īs again: *ex cubiculīs*, *ex hortīs*. And *sine* (without) belongs to the same family and takes the same case: *sine mātre suā*.

show.say: ex cubiculīs — the plural ending is -īs

check.ask: Ancillae ex ___ suīs iam discēdunt. (cubiculum, more than one)

core.text: To say where something comes from, or what it is parted from, Latin uses *ā/ab* (from, away from), *ē/ex* (out of) or *dē* (down from) with **the ablative (the 'from' form)**, *ablātīvus sēparātīvus*: *ex ātriō veniunt* = they come out of the hall; *ab Aemiliā discēdit* = she goes away from Aemilia. *Ā* and *ē* stand before consonants, *ab* and *ex* before vowels (and often before consonants as well). *Sine* (without) belongs to the same family.
*From*, *out of*, *off*, *away from* all point at a starting point: *he came from the mountain*, *the cup fell off the table*. Latin bundles them into three prepositions plus the ablative.
*Ā/ab*, *ē/ex*, *dē*, *sine* always take the ablative, whatever they mean in the sentence: *dē Deō* (about God) is still ablative.

invented.la: Servus ē vīllā ad oppidum currit.
invented.en: The slave runs out of the villa to the town.

core.text: Same ending, opposite ideas: *in hortō* (in the garden) is where something is; *ex hortō* (out of the garden) is where it comes from. The ablative does not choose; the preposition does. Read the little word first, then the ending.

more.text: From the learner's notes: origin may be physical (from the mountain), logical (disaster came from his foolishness) or in time (from April to June); the 'from' prepositions are so tied to the ablative that they keep it even when their sense has drifted — *dē* is literally 'down from' but usually means 'concerning' (*hominēs dē Deō dīcunt*). *Ā/ab* and *sine* also mark what something is separated from: *vir sine fēminā*.

Names of towns and small islands, and *domō* (from home), stand in the ablative with no preposition: *Rōmā venit*, *Tusculō venit* (r06:53.2), the question being *unde?* (from where?). *Procul ab* = far from (r06:9.1). The same *ā/ab* + ablative names the doer of a passive verb — the ablative of agent — because Latin sees the doer as the action's source. Ørberg cap. VI; A&G §401–403, §428.
